paragraphs.text: This leaf is [Meizhan](yancha:meizhan), a Fujian cultivar that came from Anxi and is also made in the Wuyi Mountains, where this tea grew. It is less famous than Rougui and Shui Xian and sits outside the four famous bushes. The lot was taken to medium oxidation, the middle ground of a [partly oxidised](oolong:definition) tea, and finished with a traditional [charcoal roast](yancha:making), which dries the leaf so it keeps.

The [Wuyi Mountains](wuyi-mountains:where-it-is) run along the border of northern Fujian and Jiangxi. The range is steep, wet and misty, and its bushes grow in [thin, stony soil](wuyi-mountains:nature) on ledges and between rocks, where the ground drains fast. A record that names only Wuyi does not say how close to the [scenic core](wuyi-mountains:zones) the leaf grew.

A [medium roast](yancha:roast-levels) is the kind of Wuyi tea made to be kept for years. What it asks of its keeper is dry, sealed storage, since damp is the main fault of stored rock tea and can turn it [green again](yancha:ageing).

brewing.text: Wuyi tea is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C, and about 5 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 120 ml gaiwan, a third to a half full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 5 to 20 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and good rock tea gives seven steeps or more. In a larger pot, use about 2 to 5 grams for 250 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker liquor with less sharpness, the roast softened and the high aroma faded.
